objectives: Explain how Einthoven's triangle and the 12 leads view the heart from different angles.
Identify each wave, segment, and interval of the PQRST complex and its normal duration.
Estimate the cardiac axis and read a basic rhythm strip systematically.

slides.title: Einthoven's triangle and the 12 leads
slides.body:
The **electrocardiogram (ECG or EKG)** records the heart's electrical activity from electrodes on the skin. **Willem Einthoven** built the first practical recorder, the **string galvanometer**, around 1901-1903, named the **P, Q, R, S, and T** deflections, and won the **Nobel Prize in 1924**. His foundational abstraction is **Einthoven's triangle**: an imaginary equilateral triangle with vertices at the **right arm (RA)**, **left arm (LA)**, and **left leg (LL)**, the heart at its center.

From these three electrodes come the three **bipolar limb leads**, each measuring the voltage between two vertices:

- **Lead I** = LA minus RA (views the heart from the left, ~0 degrees).
- **Lead II** = LL minus RA (~+60 degrees, parallel to the normal axis).
- **Lead III** = LL minus LA (~+120 degrees).

These obey **Einthoven's law**: $\text{Lead I} + \text{Lead III} = \text{Lead II}$, a built-in consistency check. From the same electrodes, **Frank Wilson** derived the **augmented unipolar limb leads** **aVR**, **aVL**, and **aVF**, each comparing one limb against the average of the other two; aVR looks from the right shoulder (~-150 degrees), aVL from the left shoulder (~-30 degrees), and aVF from the feet (~+90 degrees). Together the six limb leads view the heart in the **frontal plane** (a coronal slice), spaced about 30 degrees apart on the **hexaxial reference system**.

The remaining six leads are the **precordial (chest) leads** **V1 through V6**, placed across the chest wall by **Frank Wilson's central terminal** as the reference. They view the heart in the **horizontal (transverse) plane**:

- **V1-V2** sit over the right ventricle and septum (septal leads).
- **V3-V4** over the anterior wall (anterior leads).
- **V5-V6** over the lateral wall (lateral leads).

This is why ECG localizes disease: an inferior myocardial infarction shows changes in **II, III, and aVF**; an anterior infarction in **V1-V4**; a lateral infarction in **I, aVL, V5-V6**. The standard recording runs at **25 mm/s** paper speed with **10 mm/mV** calibration, so each small 1 mm box is **0.04 s** wide and each large 5 mm box is **0.20 s**. A wave that deflects **upward** in a given lead means depolarization is traveling **toward** that lead's positive electrode; a downward deflection means it travels away. The 12-lead ECG, assembled from just ten electrodes (four limb, six chest), thus reconstructs a three-dimensional picture of cardiac electrical activity from twelve complementary viewpoints — the single most-used test in all of cardiology.

slides.title: The PQRST complex, segments, and intervals
slides.body:
Each heartbeat inscribes a stereotyped sequence of waves that maps directly onto the conduction system. Reading them in order:

- **P wave.** Atrial depolarization, spreading from the **SA node** across both atria. Normally smooth, upright in lead II, under 0.12 s wide and under 2.5 mm tall. A broad notched P suggests left-atrial enlargement; a tall peaked P suggests right-atrial enlargement.
- **PR interval.** Measured from the start of the P wave to the start of the QRS, it spans atrial depolarization **plus** the deliberate **AV nodal delay**. Normal is **0.12-0.20 s** (3-5 small boxes). A long PR defines **first-degree AV block**; a short PR with a delta wave suggests **Wolff-Parkinson-White** pre-excitation.
- **QRS complex.** Ventricular depolarization via the **His-Purkinje system**. Because the muscle mass is large but conduction is fast, the QRS is tall but narrow, normally **under 0.12 s**. A wide QRS means slow ventricular activation — a **bundle-branch block**, a ventricular escape rhythm, or pre-excitation. By convention, **Q** is the first downward deflection, **R** the first upward, **S** the downward after R.
- **ST segment.** The plateau between QRS and T, normally **isoelectric** (flat at baseline). **ST elevation** signals acute transmural injury (**STEMI**); **ST depression** signals subendocardial ischemia or strain.
- **T wave.** Ventricular repolarization, normally upright and asymmetric (slower upstroke, faster downstroke), concordant with the QRS in most leads. **Inverted** T waves can mark ischemia; **peaked** T waves classically mark **hyperkalemia**.
- **QT interval.** From the start of QRS to the end of T — the total time of ventricular depolarization plus repolarization. Because it shortens as heart rate rises, it is corrected with **Bazett's formula**, $QT_c = \frac{QT}{\sqrt{RR}}$, where $RR$ is the R-to-R interval in seconds. A normal $QT_c$ is roughly **under 0.44 s** in men and **under 0.46 s** in women. A prolonged $QT_c$ predisposes to the dangerous polymorphic ventricular tachycardia **torsades de pointes**.
- **U wave.** A small deflection sometimes following the T wave, prominent in hypokalemia.

A few derived measures matter clinically. The **J point** is where the QRS meets the ST segment, the landmark for measuring ST shift. The **R-R interval** sets the instantaneous heart rate (rate = 300 / number of large boxes between R waves, the '300-150-100-75-60-50' rule). Mastery of these durations turns the squiggle into a precise timeline of the conduction sequence you have already learned.

slides.title: The cardiac axis and systematic rhythm reading
slides.body:
The **cardiac axis** is the net direction of ventricular depolarization in the frontal plane, the vector sum of all the instantaneous electrical forces during the QRS. A **normal axis** lies between **-30 and +90 degrees**. **Left axis deviation** (-30 to -90 degrees) accompanies left ventricular hypertrophy, left anterior fascicular block, and inferior infarcts; **right axis deviation** (+90 to +180 degrees) accompanies right ventricular hypertrophy, lateral infarcts, and pulmonary disease.

A fast bedside estimate uses two leads. Look at the **net QRS deflection** (positive minus negative) in **lead I** and in **lead aVF**:

- Lead I positive **and** aVF positive: **normal axis** (the vector points down and to the left, toward both positive electrodes).
- Lead I positive, aVF negative: **left axis deviation** (vector points up-left).
- Lead I negative, aVF positive: **right axis deviation** (vector points down-right).
- Both negative: **extreme axis** ('northwest' axis).

A more precise method finds the **isoelectric lead** (the one where positive and negative QRS areas are most equal); the axis is then perpendicular to that lead's orientation on the hexaxial system, pointing toward whichever lead is most positive.

**Systematic rhythm reading** prevents missed diagnoses. A reliable order of questions:

- **1. Rate.** Normal sinus is 60-100 bpm; below 60 is **bradycardia**, above 100 is **tachycardia**. Use the large-box rule or count complexes in a 6-second strip times 10.
- **2. Rhythm regularity.** Are R-R intervals constant? An irregularly irregular rhythm with no clear P waves suggests **atrial fibrillation**.
- **3. P waves.** Is there one upright P (in lead II) before every QRS? This confirms sinus origin.
- **4. PR interval.** Constant and normal, or prolonged (first-degree block), progressively lengthening then dropping (Wenckebach, **Mobitz I**), or intermittently dropping with constant PR (**Mobitz II**)? No relationship at all between P and QRS means **third-degree (complete) heart block**.
- **5. QRS width.** Narrow (supraventricular origin) or wide (ventricular origin or aberrant conduction)?
- **6. ST/T changes.** Elevation, depression, T-wave inversion?

Applying this checklist to every tracing — rate, rhythm, axis, intervals, morphology — is the discipline that lets a cardiologist distinguish a benign sinus tachycardia from a life-threatening **ventricular tachycardia** at a glance, and it ties together everything from Einthoven's geometry to the Purkinje anatomy underneath.

question.question: Which segment of the ECG measures atrial depolarization PLUS the deliberate delay at the AV node, and is normally 0.12 to 0.20 seconds?
question.explanation: The PR interval runs from the start of the P wave to the start of the QRS, encompassing atrial depolarization and the AV nodal delay; its normal range is 0.12-0.20 s. A prolonged PR defines first-degree AV block. The QT interval is depolarization plus repolarization, the QRS is ventricular depolarization, and the ST segment is the isoelectric plateau.

hints: It begins at the P wave and ends as the ventricles begin to depolarize.
Its main contributor is the slow conduction through the AV node.
slides.workedSolution: The PR interval (0.12-0.20 s) reflects atrial depolarization plus AV nodal delay. Prolongation beyond 0.20 s is first-degree AV block; the AV node is the dominant contributor to its duration.

question.question: On a standard ECG, the R waves are separated by exactly 4 large boxes. Using the rule that one large box is 0.20 s, what is the heart rate in beats per minute?
question.hint: Rate = 300 divided by the number of large boxes between R waves, or equivalently 60 divided by the R-R interval in seconds.

question.question: A patient has a measured QT interval of 0.40 s and an R-R interval of 1.00 s. Using Bazett's formula QTc = QT / sqrt(RR), compute the corrected QT in seconds.
question.hint: The square root of an R-R of 1.00 s is 1.00, so QTc equals QT divided by 1.

question.question: Using the quick two-lead method, a QRS that is net POSITIVE in lead I but net NEGATIVE in lead aVF indicates which cardiac axis?
question.explanation: Lead I positive means the vector points leftward (toward lead I's positive electrode); aVF negative means it points upward (away from the feet). Up and to the left is left axis deviation (-30 to -90 degrees). Normal axis is positive in both; right axis is negative in I and positive in aVF; extreme axis is negative in both.

hints: Positive in I points the vector to the left; negative in aVF points it upward.
Up-and-to-the-left corresponds to a negative axis angle.
slides.workedSolution: I positive (leftward) + aVF negative (upward) = a vector pointing up and to the left = left axis deviation. This pattern appears with LV hypertrophy, left anterior fascicular block, and inferior MI.

question.question: An irregular pulse with no P waves
question.prompt: A 72-year-old reports palpitations and lightheadedness. Her ECG shows an irregularly irregular rhythm at about 130 bpm, narrow QRS complexes, and no discernible P waves before each QRS, with a wavy baseline instead. Walk through the systematic rhythm-reading checklist (rate, regularity, P waves, PR, QRS width) as applied to this tracing, state the most likely rhythm diagnosis, and explain why the absence of organized P waves and the irregular ventricular response are the hallmark features. What does the narrow QRS tell you about where the impulses are originating?
